scenarios.title: The Empty Seat
situation: The deadline is tomorrow at noon. Your four-person project is finally assembled, polished, and ready to submit — except for one thing: the teammate who was supposed to deliver the analysis section.
She messaged you an hour ago. Her father was hospitalized last night in another city; she has been on a train since dawn. She is not asking for anything. She is just telling you why she went silent.
Her name is on the cover page. Her section is not in the document.
scenarios.prompt: Your teammate did not contribute to the project because of a family emergency. The deadline is tomorrow. How do you handle the credit?

freeText.prompt: What would you actually do — and why?

choices.label: Remove her name. Grades and credit should reflect the work actually done.
choices.consequence: The submission is technically accurate. Your teammate sees the updated cover page from a hospital corridor at midnight. The project survives. Something else does not.

choices.label: Give her full credit anyway — she would have contributed if not for the emergency.
choices.consequence: The report goes in with both names and one phantom section. It gets the highest mark of your semester. Your teammate finds out, and is mortified — the grade now sits on her conscience like a debt she never agreed to.

choices.label: Give partial credit, tell the professor the situation honestly, and rebuild the timeline with her.
choices.consequence: You email the professor the facts and a fair split — analysis section marked incomplete, extension requested or credit adjusted. The professor, human after all, agrees to let her submit her section late for partial marks. Your teammate catches the next train home lighter than she boarded it.

choices.label: Say nothing, submit as is, sort it out later.
choices.consequence: It works — technically. The grade posts a week later and the group chat develops a silence with a shape to it. The unspoken thing grows teeth.

insight.principle: Most real dilemmas are solved at the honest middle, negotiated in daylight — not at the poles.
insight.source: Krishna's statecraft: before choosing between two bad options, widen the options.

scenarios.title: The Purchased Essay
situation: You discover — because he told you, laughing with relief at a party — that your closest friend bought his final term paper online. The course is graded on a curve.
The professor suspects nothing. Your friend is not a bad person; he was drowning in four deadlines and a part-time job, and he took the exit ramp that was offered to him by an anonymous website.
Your own grade rises or falls with his, and with everyone else's.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do about your friend's purchased paper?

choices.label: Report him to the professor. A curve is a shared resource.
choices.consequence: The inquiry is quiet and quick. He is failed on the paper — and suspended from the program for a term. The curve is clean. So is the seat where your friend used to sit in the front row.

choices.label: Confront him privately and push him to withdraw the paper and resubmit his own work.
choices.consequence: He goes pale, then furious, then — two days later — grateful. He withdraws the purchased file and turns in his own rough draft with a note to the professor about the delay. He loses ten points. He keeps his degree, his integrity, and his friend.

choices.label: Say nothing. His paper, his risk, his conscience.
choices.consequence: You keep the friendship and lose the argument with yourself. Every curve-graded exam this term, a small voice asks what your silence was worth — and you find you already know the exchange rate.

choices.label: Send an anonymous tip to the professor.
choices.consequence: The inquiry happens without your name attached. He never learns who tipped the professor — but he stops telling you things, having somehow guessed. Justice was served, and the friendship was billed for it quietly.

insight.principle: Truth has costs, and still outranks convenience — but how you tell it is a moral choice of its own.
insight.source: Yudhishthira: the man who never lied, asked to spend his truth like coin.

scenarios.title: The Viral Jest
situation: Someone in your class made a meme mocking a quiet classmate's stutter. It is funny in the way that makes your stomach drop while you laugh. It is now in three group chats and climbing.
The classmate has not seen it — as far as anyone knows. The person who made it is popular, funny, and — this is the part that complicates it — someone who once stood up for you when it counted.
Three people have already shared it. One of them just asked you: “your turn.”
scenarios.prompt: The post is one share away from your feed. What do you do?

choices.label: Share it. Refusing will just make me the next meme.
choices.consequence: You tap share. The meme reaches two hundred more screens by night, and one of them, finally, is his. He stops raising his hand in class — and you learn that silence and participation invoice separately, but they both bill.

choices.label: Refuse to share — and message the maker privately: this one crosses a line, take it down.
choices.consequence: “Relax, it's a joke,” he replies. But an hour later the meme quietly disappears from the chats where it started. The classmate never knows how close it came. Sometimes the win is invisible, and is a win anyway.

choices.label: Call it out publicly in the group: ‘this is bullying, and you know it.’
choices.consequence: The chat splits — two people agree with you, three mock you, the meme-maker goes cold. The post dies by evening. Your name is now ‘too serious’ for a month. The classmate hears about the argument — and about who stood in it.

choices.label: Report the post silently and stay out of the social crossfire.
choices.consequence: The platform removes it in two days — after two more hundred views. You kept your hands clean and your weekends social. The classmate's stutter got two more days of material.

insight.principle: A word spoken in a hall stays in the hall; a post speaks to ten thousand halls. Scale changes the ethics.
insight.source: The dice hall at Hastinapura: humiliation staged before a crowd is a wound that does not close.

scenarios.title: The Missed Milestone
situation: The client demo was scheduled for Friday. It is Friday, 9 a.m., and the feature is not ready — because of a scheduling error you made three weeks ago, quietly, when you moved two critical reviews into the same week as the fest.
Nobody knows the error was yours. The team thinks the delay was the API team. The client sponsor has asked for a call at noon: ‘Walk me through what happened.’
Your junior, Priya, is already drafting a slide that shows the API team's timeline in red.
scenarios.prompt: The sponsor asks what happened. What do you tell them?

freeText.prompt: Your answer, in your own words.

choices.label: Let the API timeline speak. Their delay, their names on the slide.
choices.consequence: The call goes smoothly. The API team's lead, blindsided, spends a week repairing relations you spent. Priya watches you let a false slide stand — and quietly updates her notes on what kind of leader you are.

choices.label: Own it fully: the error was mine, here is the recovery plan and the safeguard so it never repeats.
choices.consequence: You present the miss and the mistake in one breath — yours — then a two-week recovery plan with checkpoints. The sponsor's respect visibly rises; trust, it turns out, compounds on admissions. Your team stops sliding blame around the room and starts shipping.

choices.label: Describe the external factors honestly but vaguely — ‘a scheduling conflict’ — without naming yourself.
choices.consequence: ‘A scheduling conflict’ is true the way a shadow is shaped like its object. The sponsor accepts it. The phrase costs you nothing today and a little of you every day after — you now maintain two versions of the story, and stories multiply.

choices.label: Minimize: ‘we're basically on track, just a small bump’ — and push the demo a week.
choices.consequence: The sponsor smiles and agrees to a week. Three weeks later the second demo slips too, and the word ‘basically’ has become a running joke in their office. Optimism without a ledger reads, eventually, as evasion.

insight.principle: A leader's confession is the team's permission to be honest.
insight.source: Yudhishthira refused to blame the dice, the hall, or fate — he owned the stake he chose to raise.

scenarios.title: The Inflated Invoice
situation: You are three months into your first job. Reconciling the month's invoices, you notice the client billing has been padded — hours that were not worked, licenses that were never bought. Small amounts, systematically. Your manager approved every line.
The manager who hired you. The manager who defended your raise last month. The manager everyone else says is ‘carrying the whole team on his back.’
The company handbook has a compliance hotline. The hotline reports to a department your manager lunchs with.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do about the inflated invoices?

choices.label: Report to compliance, in writing, with the ledger attached.
choices.consequence: The audit runs for six quiet weeks. The padding stops; your manager is ‘reassigned’; the office learns a new fact about you. The numbers were right. The cost was real. Both things stay true.

choices.label: Talk to him first — one private conversation: ‘this has to stop, and I have to be able to say it did.’
choices.consequence: He listens, goes very still, and says ‘leave it with me.’ The next invoice is clean, and so are the two after it. Whether that was correction or concealment, you cannot prove — and you carry the question like a stone in your shoe.

choices.label: Ignore it. It is above your pay grade, and the client has not complained.
choices.consequence: You stop reconciling invoices so carefully. Two years later the scheme is a scandal with a newspaper, and the audit trail runs straight through the months you noticed and said nothing. ‘Junior’, the timeline notes, ‘but not blind.’

choices.label: Document everything quietly, tell no one, and wait for a safer moment.
choices.consequence: Your folder grows: screenshots, dates, amounts. You tell yourself it is preparation, not complicity, and some months that is even true. The folder is powerful. So is the habit of watching a slow wrong while taking notes.

insight.principle: Silence in the presence of a slow wrong is a slow yes.
insight.source: Bhishma in the dice hall: the epic's greatest study of what respectable silence costs.

scenarios.title: The Confession Call
situation: Your best friend failed a crucial exam — the one his parents moved cities for. He told them he passed. He told you the truth the same night, shaking.

Three weeks later his mother calls you, voice bright with relief: “You were with him after the results, no? Tell me again — how did he take the good news?” She wants to hear it from the friend she trusts.
Retaking the exam is possible in six months. The lie unravels the day results are posted publicly.
scenarios.prompt: His mother is waiting on the line. What do you say?

freeText.prompt: What comes out of your mouth?

choices.label: Play along — ‘he was so happy.’ A loyal friend covers first, fixes later.
choices.consequence: She laughs with relief and thanks the gods and you. Your voice on that call becomes one more brick in a wall that falls on her in six months — now with your name in the rubble. Loyalty, it turns out, can be spent on the wrong side of a lie.

choices.label: Tell her gently: ‘Aunty, he didn't pass — and he's already planning the retake. Please let him tell you the rest.’
choices.consequence: The line goes silent, then very quiet. She says ‘thank you for telling me’ in a voice that means the opposite of thank you. But by evening the house is dealing with the real problem instead of the real lie — and your friend, furious at first, sleeps without the weight for the first time in weeks.

choices.label: Deflect: ‘I think his results are his to share, Aunty — talk to him tonight.’
choices.consequence: You neither lie nor betray — you hand the hot iron back to the two people who must hold it eventually. She hangs up puzzled. The conversation that night is harder than the one your friend rehearsed for, and maybe more honest than either of you planned.

choices.label: Tell her you'll call back — then give him one hour to confess himself, or you will.
choices.consequence: He confesses in forty minutes — furious, terrified, and on his own feet. His mother hears it from her son instead of a phone tree. You get a two-week silence and, at the end of it, a friend who knows exactly what you will and will not carry for him.

insight.principle: Loyalty that requires your dishonesty is spending your dharma to protect another's secret.
insight.source: Karna and Duryodhana: friendship at its fiercest, and its most expensive.

scenarios.title: The Storm Call
situation: You are the student coordinator of the college cultural fest. Three hundred tickets sold. Doors open tomorrow at 9 a.m.
The 8 p.m. weather update just moved the storm from ‘possible’ to ‘likely, evening, with gusts.’ The main stage is an open ground. The covered hall fits 120 people and has terrible acoustics.
The organizing committee is split down the middle: ‘cancel, safety first’ versus ‘we bet the forecast is wrong, we cannot refund 300 tickets.’ Everyone is looking at you.
scenarios.prompt: The committee needs your call tonight. What do you decide?

freeText.prompt: Give your call and your reasoning.

choices.label: Cancel outright. Refund everyone. Safety is the whole event.
choices.consequence: The refunds cost the fest its entire year's budget, and two sponsors grumble publicly. The storm, for the record, arrives at 6 p.m. and folds a stage truss onto the empty ground. Nobody died. The committee ages a year. The math holds.

choices.label: Go ahead — but restructure: indoor capacity plan, staggered entry, live-streamed main acts, storm protocol with marshals.
choices.consequence: The fest runs at half comfort and full preparation. The storm arrives; the marshals move 300 people through a plan they rehearsed at midnight. Two acts stream from the hall to the half-empty ground. It is not the fest you planned — it is the one that survives it.

choices.label: Wait for the 5 a.m. update and decide then — with both contingency plans drafted tonight.
choices.consequence: You sleep three hours and decide at dawn against clearer data. The delay costs you the morning logistics, and the vendors charge for the chaos. But the call you make at 5:40 a.m. is the right call, made with one more satellite pass of evidence.

choices.label: Put it to a vote of the ticket-holders — let the crowd own the risk.
choices.consequence: Sixty percent vote ‘go ahead’ — of course they do; they are not the ones holding the liability. You now have a mandate and no captain. When the gusts arrive, three hundred people discover simultaneously that democracy is not a shelter plan.

insight.principle: In crisis, a decent plan now beats a perfect plan after the storm — and owning the call matters more than the odds.
insight.source: The war councils of Kurukshetra: decide under uncertainty, then carry the decision publicly.

scenarios.title: The Senior Tradition
situation: It is 11 p.m. in the second-year corridor. The first-years are being run through the ‘welcome tradition’ — reciting slogans, doing squats, one boy being made to apologize to a senior's shoes.
Most are laughing the way people laugh on boats: holding the rail. One boy — you know him from the library; he barely talks to anyone — is not laughing at all.
If you intervene alone, you become the target. If it is reported, nobody will say who did. The seniors running it include your project partner and your hostel floor-mate.
scenarios.prompt: The corridor is watching. What do you do?

freeText.prompt: Your decision — in your own words.

choices.label: Step in now, alone: ‘Enough. Let him sit down.’
choices.consequence: The corridor goes quiet. ‘Relax,’ someone says, and you do not. The tradition limps to a close early; the boy from the library disappears to his room — leaving, you notice later, a thank-you note under your door. You are ‘the funny one's project’ for a week. It was worth it.

choices.label: Report it to the anti-ragging committee tonight, anonymously, with names.
choices.consequence: A notice appears on the department board; two seniors are summoned; the tradition dies by paperwork. It is less dramatic than a corridor confrontation and more permanent. The first-years never learn which quiet classmate ended it — which was the point.

choices.label: Quietly gather three others tonight, then confront the seniors as a group tomorrow.
choices.consequence: Four of you meet the seniors at tea, all politeness and steel: the tradition ends, or the committee gets the names. Numbers change the arithmetic of courage. The tradition ends quietly by Friday — and you have built a coalition that will outlast this one corridor.

choices.label: Walk past. Everyone went through it; the system self-corrects.
choices.consequence: You walk past, and the corridor keeps its noise. The boy from the library stops coming to the library. ‘Everyone went through it’ turns out to be a sentence said by everyone who walked past — the tradition corrects nothing, it recruits.

insight.principle: Tradition is just a decision that stopped admitting it was one.
insight.source: Yudhishthira at the dice game: ‘it is the rule’ is the oldest excuse in the epic — and the costliest.
